author: Grace Chen
title: Suriname Declared Malaria-Free by WHO | Latest News
text:
suriname Achieves Malaria-Free Status, a Landmark Victory for the Amazon Region Suriname has become the first country in the Amazon region to be declared malaria-free by the World Health Association (WHO), marking a monumental achievement in global health and a beacon of hope for disease elimination in challenging environments. This historic certification, announced today, culminates nearly 70 years of dedicated effort by the government and people of Suriname to eradicate the mosquito-borne illness across it’s diverse landscapes.
A Milestone in Global Health
The WHO’s certification recognizes that Suriname has demonstrably interrupted the chain of indigenous malaria transmission nationwide for at least the past three consecutive years. This accomplishment brings the total number of countries officially declared malaria-free to 46, including 12 in the Americas.”WHO congratulates Suriname on this remarkable achievement,” stated Dr. Tedros adhanom Ghebreyesus,WHO Director-General. “This certification is a powerful affirmation of the principle that everyone-regardless of nationality, background, or migration status-deserves global access to malaria diagnosis and treatment. Suriname’s steadfast commitment to health equity serves as an inspiration to all countries striving for a malaria-free future.”
Years of Dedicated Effort
Suriname’s journey toward malaria elimination began in the 1950s, initially focusing on densely populated coastal areas. Early strategies relied heavily on indoor spraying with the pesticide DDT and widespread antimalarial treatment. by the 1960s, malaria had been successfully contained in these coastal regions, allowing attention to shift to the country’s vast forested interior, home to diverse indigenous and tribal communities.
Did you know? -DDT, while effective against mosquitoes, has been banned or restricted in many countries due to its environmental impact and potential harm to human health. Suriname initially relied on DDT before adopting more enduring strategies.
Though, the interior presented unique challenges. Traditional open-style homes offered limited protection against mosquitoes, diminishing the effectiveness of indoor spraying. in 1974, malaria control efforts in the interior were decentralized to Medische Zending, Suriname’s primary healthcare service. This pivotal move involved recruiting and training healthcare workers from local communities to provide early diagnosis and treatment – a strategy that proved crucial for long-term success.
overcoming Obstacles: Mining and Mobile Populations
The rise of mining activities, especially gold mining, introduced a new hurdle in the early 2000s. The influx of workers traveling between malaria-endemic areas led to a surge in cases, peaking at over 15,000 in 2001 – the highest transmission rate in the Americas at the time.
Reader question: -What other innovative strategies could be employed to combat malaria in remote and hard-to-reach populations, drawing inspiration from suriname’s success?
A turning point came in 2005 with support from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. This funding dramatically expanded diagnostic capacity through improved microscopy and the introduction of rapid diagnostic tests, particularly for mobile populations. concurrently,artemisinin-based treatments with primaquine were implemented through studies led by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO),under the Amazon Malaria Initiative (AMI-RAVREDA),with support from the United States. Preventive measures,including the distribution of insecticide-treated nets funded by the Global Fund,were also strengthened.
by 2006, significant progress had been made in reducing malaria among indigenous populations. The focus then shifted to high-risk mobile populations in remote mining areas. Suriname innovatively established a network of “Malaria Service Deliverers,” recruited directly from the mining communities themselves. these trained and supervised community workers provided free malaria diagnosis,treatment,and prevention services,effectively bridging access gaps in previously hard-to-reach regions.
Universal Access and sustained Commitment
suriname’s success hinged on ensuring universal access to diagnosis and treatment, regardless of legal status. Nationwide malaria screening, including at border crossings, further bolstered these efforts.The last locally transmitted case of Plasmodium falciparum malaria was recorded in 2018, followed by the final Plasmodium vivax case in 2021.
“Suriname did what was needed to eliminate malaria-detecting and treating every case quickly, investigating to prevent spread, and engaging communities,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, Director of PAHO. “This certification reflects years of sustained effort, especially reaching remote areas.It means future generations can grow up free from this potentially deadly disease.”
The government of Suriname has demonstrated unwavering commitment through the establishment of the National Malaria Elimination Taskforce, Malaria Programme, and Malaria Elimination Fund, alongside robust cross-border collaboration with Brazil, Guyana, and French Guiana. Since 2016, Suriname has also participated in the “Elimination 2025” initiative, a WHO-led effort to accelerate malaria elimination globally.
Dr.Amar Ramadhin, Minister of Health of Suriname, emphasized the broader benefits of this achievement: “Being malaria-free means that our population is no longer at risk from malaria. Furthermore, eliminating malaria will have positive effects on our healthcare sector, boost the economy, and enhance tourism.” He also acknowledged the need for continued vigilance, stating, “We must continue to take the necessary measures to prevent the reintroduction of malaria. We are proud that our communities are now protected,and we look forward to welcoming more visitors to our beautiful suriname-while remaining fully committed to safeguarding these hard-won gains.”
Suriname’s triumph serves as a powerful demonstration that malaria elimination is achievable, even in the challenging context of the Amazon basin and other tropical continental countries. This certification will significantly advance PAHO’s Disease Elimination Initiative, which aims to eliminate over 30 communicable diseases, including malaria, throughout the Americas by 2030.
